- When sentiment is strongly bullish (≥0.67) and model forecast is flat or rising slowly, adjust upward by 1–3% to account for sentiment-driven momentum.
- After a sharp spike in price (e.g., >5% from prior day), model should not overreact — cap forecast increase to 2–3% per day to avoid overshoot.
- If official event net supply is negative and sentiment is bearish, model should not ignore the bearish signal — reduce forecast slope or add downward bias.
- When sentiment swings from bullish to bearish within 3–5 days, model should adjust forecast slope downward, especially if true outcome shows mean reversion.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome deviates >5% from initial forecast, check if sentiment history shows divergence — if so, apply a “sentiment correction” by aligning forecast to sentiment trend.
- If official events are frequent and supply net is negative, model should not assume price will continue rising — expect mean reversion or volatility decay after 5–7 days.
- If sentiment is consistently negative (≤-0.5) and forecast is rising, reduce forecast slope by 10–20% to avoid false optimism.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome shows early sharp rise followed by decline, model should not over-forecast the peak — cap forecast at 2–3 days after peak.
